item.title: Your Child's Passport to the World: Essential Travel Documents from Germany
item.description: As Turkish families and expats living in Germany, we often find ourselves navigating a beautiful blend of cultures and, of course, a good deal of German bureaucracy. While we love the freedom of travel that comes with living in the heart of Europe, one area that consistently causes stress for us, especially when traveling with children, is the mountain of documents required. I’ve heard countless stories, and experienced a few myself, of families being delayed or even denied boarding because of missing paperwork for their little ones. It’s a situation no one wants to be in, particularly after months of planning that perfect family vacation!

item.title: Raising Children: Space, Safety and Independence
item.description:
This post is part of the “Turkey or Germany?” series. It is not a contest of better or worse; it is about two different cultures and what to expect. Series intro: Before you start comparing

Giving my children a better future was my number one criterion. After moving here I understood better that this is not only about education.

One park in Istanbul, 50 children
#

When I lived in Istanbul there was a park in front of my home, actually two parks next to each other. When we went out at the weekend, or when I went for an evening walk, there were, without exaggeration, more than 50 children in that park. Little space, lots of children; everyone squeezed into the same place.

item.title: Education and the Ausbildung System: University Is Not the Only Path in Germany
item.description:
This post is part of the “Turkey or Germany?” series. It is not a contest of better or worse; it is about two different cultures and what to expect. Series intro: Before you start comparing

My children’s future was the most important criterion in my decision to move, and education is at the heart of it.

The Turkish side
#

In Turkey, nurseries and private schools are very expensive; an ordinary employee can end up spending half of their salary on them. Everyone gets a university degree, yet the country is full of unemployed graduates.
